background.definition: Breast cancer is an abnormal growth or tumor of the breast usually detected on mammography or by clinical or breast self-examination.

list.listitem: In 2020, CDC estimates that there will be 276,480 new cases of breast cancer will be diagnosed in women, and 42,170 are expected to die of breast cancer.

In 2016 in the US, incidence rates in white women were higher than in black women (125 vs. 122.6/100,000) or Hispanic women (93.7/100,000). However, 5 years survival rates are higher for white woman (90%) and Hispanic woman (90.3%) than for black women (80%).
Breast cancer Incidence rates in women decreased 3.5% per year from 2001 to 2004, the first decrease observed in 20 years.

This decrease may in part be due to the decrease in use of postmenopausal hormones; data from the Women’s Health Initiative show a decreased incidence in breast cancer as hormone use decreased, not caused by changes in mammography use.
There were 6.94 new cases of late-stage diagnosis breast cancer per 100,000 women in 2003, which is a decrease from previous years.
The chance of a woman having invasive breast cancer at some time during her life is approximately 1 in 8, while the chance of dying from breast cancer is approximately 1 in 35.
Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in women. There were 40,460 breast cancer-related deaths in 2007 (15% of all cancer types).
Breast cancer-related mortality is declining because of early diagnosis and treatment.

Analysis of administrative data found that the cost per patient in the US during the year following diagnosis was approximately $60,000 for stage 0 disease, $82,000 for stage I/II disease, $130,000 for stage III and $135,000 for stage IV disease.
Women with disabilities have higher breast cancer mortality rates and are less likely to undergo standard therapy after breast-conserving surgery than other women.

The genomic landscape of breast cancers is composed of a handful of commonly mutated gene “mountains” (eg, BRCA1 and BRCA2) and a much larger number of gene “hills” such as PALB2 that are mutated at low frequency.

Risk factors for breast cancer can be integrated into an etiologic model comprising three principal components: the number of mammary tissue-specific stem cells (determined in early life); growth-enhancing mammotropic hormones (that affect the number of target cells and the likelihood of retention of spontaneous mutations and their expansion); and differentiation of mammary tissue-specific stem cells (occurs during pregnancy and is protective).

Based on 20 year follow-up of the large Women's Health Initiative study, for women who have had a hysterectomy estrogen replacement therapy alone decreases the risk of invasive breast cancer (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.65-0.93) and of breast cancer mortality (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.37-0.97). However, estrogen plus progesterone was associated with a statistically significant higher breast cancer incidence (HR = 1.28; 1.13-1.45), but no significant difference in breast cancer mortality.
A Dutch population study investigating the risk of breast cancer in women undergoing IVF treatment found no increase in risk associated with IVF.

Follow-up of over 500,000 women in the Swedish population registry who had levonorgestrel IUDs inserted demonstrated a small increase in risk of subsequent breast cancer (approimately 1.5/10,000 person-years).
See for risk factors; most women with breast cancer do not have risk factors.

Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS): the former is the most common in situ tumor, and arises in the major lactiferous ducts. It tends to be more localized. LCIS arises from the terminal duct lobular apparatus and shows a diffuse distribution in the breast.
Invasive ductal carcinoma (70% of cases): highest prevalence in perimenopausal or early postmenopausal women; composed of heterogeneous cells arranged in single rows; multiple subtypes.
Invasive lobular carcinoma: composed of small homogenous cells that invade the stroma; often multifocal, bilateral, and estrogen and progesterone receptor positive.
Medullary carcinoma: less common and occurs in younger women.
Mucinous carcinoma: also uncommon and usually occurs in older women.

Estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and Herceptin protein (HER)2/neu (a protooncogene in the epidermal growth factors receptor family) play a role in tumorigenesis and regulation of breast cancer. They are also important in treatment. ER-positive cancers undergo apoptosis with estrogen withdrawal. HER2/neu, overexpressed in 20% to 30% of breast cancers and associated with a high histologic grade and poor clinical outcome, can be the site for targeted treatment using monoclonal antibodies (trastuzumab) or small molecule inhibitors (lapatinib).

list.listitem: The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) most recent update (2024) recommends screening mammography every 2 years for all women aged 40 to 74 years.B
The precise age at which to discontinue screening mammography is uncertain; women with comorbid conditions that limit their life expectancy are unlikely to benefit from screening.B

Chemoprevention (tamoxifen or raloxifene) should be discussed with high-risk women; breast cancer risk and death are decreased, cardiovascular risks are increased, and all-cause mortality is not improved. B Chemoprevention is not recommended in women at average risk for breast cancer development. A

An international RCT (IBIS II) of anastrozole vs. placebo in 3864 high-risk post-menopausal women demonstrated a reduction in risk of developing breast cancer in those women taking hormone therapy. The NNT was 62 to prevent one cancer over a 5-year period, although there was no proven reduction in mortality. B

The USPSTF recommends against teaching breast self-examination (BSE). The Canadian Task Force on Preventive Care also recommends that routine teaching of BSE be excluded from the periodic health examination for women between the ages of 40 and 69 years.
The USPSTF concludes that the evidence is insufficient to assess the benefits and harms of CBE in addition to screening mammography in women 40 years or older.

As of 2024, the USPSTF recommends biennial screening mammography for all women between the ages of 40 and 74 years. The relative risk reduction of breast cancer mortality due to mammographic screening is 15% to 20% for women between the ages of 40 and 49 years with an absolute risk reduction of only 0.05% (number needed to screen = 1900 for 10 years to prolong 1 life). This compares with an NNT of 1339 for women between the ages of 50 and 59 years, and 377 for women between the ages of 60 and 69 years. After the 2009 USPSTF update changed mammography recommendation for women 40 to 49 from a "B" to a "C," the rate of mammography did not change, though. USPSTF recommendation released in 2019 did not change this recommendation.

The American Cancer Society recommends that women have routine annual mammograms from age 45 to 54 years of age, and after that may switch to a biennial (every 2 year) schedule until their life expectancy is less than 10 years. Shared decision-making is recommended for women 40 to 44 years.

The Canadian Task Force for Preventive Health Care recommends mammography every 2 years from ages 50 to 74 years, while the UK National Screening Committee recommends it every 3 years for women age 50 to 70 years. The American College of Physicians recommends mammography every 2 years from ages 50 to 74 years.
The 2020 European Guidelines on screening propose digital mammography every 2 to 3 years from age 45 to 75 but acknowledge lack of evidence for those outside the age range from 50 to 70 years.

Screening leads to overdiagnosis and overtreatment, with an estimated 30% increase, or an absolute risk increase of 0.5%. This leads women to overestimate the likelihood that their life has been saved by mammography (which is actually only about 10% of women diagnosed with breast cancer). Current estimates are that approximately 2/3 of the reduction in breast cancer mortality over the past several decades is due to advances in therapy, not due to widespread screening. An analysis of data from the past 30 years in the US found a large increase in the rate of detection of early stage cancers, but very little corresponding decrease in the rate of late-stage cancers. Their estimate is similar to others, finding that between 22% and 31% of breast cancers represent overdiagnosis (50,000-70,000 women per year).

A review of almost 36,000 women undergoing population breast screening between ages 50-74 in the US estimated that the rate of overdiagnosis was 1 in 7. This was attributed to screen detected lesions which would not have become invasive and others where the pace of the lesion meant that other co-morbidity in the individual would have been the life limiting factor.

An analysis found that for 1000 40-year-old women screened annually for 10 years: 0.1 to 1.6 will avoid dying from breast cancer, 510 to 690 will have at least 1 false alarm, with 60 to 80 undergoing a biopsy. Up to 11 will be overdiagnosed and treated without the possibility of benefit.For this reason, although the USPSTF made the 2024 recommendation that women should be considered for mammography from age 40, there is a case for shared decision making weighing up risks and benefits of screening. Among 1,000 50-year-old women: 0.3 to 3.2 will avoid dying from breast cancer, 490 to 670 will have at least 1 false alarm, with 70 to 100 undergoing a biopsy; 3 to 14 will be overdiagnosed and treated without the possibility of benefit. Among 1,000 60-year-old women: 0.5 to 4.9 will avoid dying from breast cancer, 390 to 540 will have at least 1 false alarm, with 50 to 70 undergoing a biopsy; 6 to 20 will be overdiagnosed and treated without the possibility of benefit.

A review of patients diagnosed on screening above age 70 years demonstrated increasing levels of 'overdiagnosis' with increasing age, defined as diagnosis of breast cancer which would not have caused symptoms in the remaining lifespan. Estimated overdiagnosis rate was 31% in age 70-74, 47% age 75-84 and 51% in those over 85 years. This would argue against screening in the over 70 years age group

Approximately 1 in 3 women will have a false-positive screening result and 1 in 27 women will have a breast cancer diagnosis following a screening mammogram in women between the ages of 40 years and 69 years during a 10-year screening period. Another study found that women receiving an annual mammogram for 10 years beginning at age 40 years have a 61% chance of a false positive during that time.
A US survey found that 27% of women preferred to delay screening until age 50, and when given additional information about potential benefits and harms that rose to 38%.

Digital mammography is more sensitive than film mammography for women younger than 50 years, premenopausal and perimenopausal women, and women with dense breasts. It does not result in more unnecessary biopsies, but is between 1.5 times and 4 times as costly as film mammography. The survival benefit is almost certainly less impressive than the difference in accuracy.
Adding ultrasound to mammography results in increased false positives without an increase in cancer detection and is not routinely recommended.
For women with dense breasts, supplemental screening with contrast enhanced mammography has been demonstrated to be equivalent to use of MRI in a study of 9361 women.

The age at which to discontinue screening mammography is uncertain. Only 2 RCTs enrolled women older than 69 years, and no trials enrolled women older than 74 years. Older women face a higher probability of developing and dying from breast cancer but also have a greater chance of dying from other causes. Women with comorbid conditions that limit their life expectancy are unlikely to benefit from screening.
Hormone therapy reduces mammography sensitivity and breast augmentation also reduces sensitivity but does not appear to increase the false-positive rate.

A cohort study found an association between not opting for breast cancer screening and increased mortality. While it may be in part a consequence of failure to screen, it is more likely due to healthy volunteer bias. A large UK randomized trial found that women declining participation in a screening trial had far higher all cause mortality than those who volunteered for the study.

Screening with MRI results in a much higher biopsy rate than mammography. Although there may be an increase in the number of early cancers detected, the evidence suggests that overdiagnosis and overtreatment may outweigh benefits. The USPSTF found that evidence is insufficient to assess the additional benefits and harms of either digital mammography or MRI instead of film mammography as screening modalities for breast cancer.

A randomized trial found that supplemental MRI screening for women with very dense breasts, compared with mammography alone every 2 years, significantly reduces the likelihood of an interval cancer, from 5.0/1000 to 2.5/1000 in the intention-to-treat population and to 0.8/1000 in the per-protocol population. However, false positive results were common, and there were more overall cancers and more early-stage cancers detected in the MRI group, raising the concern that many of these may have been present but growing slowly and indolently (so-called overdiagnosed cancers).

Clinically significant mutations of BRCA1 and BRCA2 are associated with increased susceptibility for breast cancer. Evidence is lacking for the benefits or harms of screening for these genetic mutations in the general population. The USPSTF recommends genetic counseling and possible screening for high-risk women (). 2019 advice is that family physicians should use risk assessment tools to select women for onward referral for genetic counselling.
A validated online calculator (B-RST) is available to determine if a woman is at sufficient risk for one of the BRCA mutations to require genetic counseling and possibly BRCA testing.

Conduct routine periodic risk assessments, and engage in discussions with individuals regarding the benefits and harms of breast cancer screening.The Gail Risk Calculator is a clinical tool that can guide the determination of a woman’s risk for breast cancer and can influence her screening preference.
High soy intake is associated with a small relative reduction in breast cancer risk in premenopausal women. Breastfeeding also reduces the incidence of breast cancer.
Vitamin D is not effective for preventing cancer (or cardiovascular disease).
Bilateral prophylactic mastectomy (BPM) prevents 1 breast cancer for every 6 high-risk women who undergo BPM and prevents 1 breast cancer-related death for every 25 high-risk women who undergo BPM.

A recent Cochrane review questions whether the improved survival observed with risk-reducing mastectomy is in part due to lack of control of confounding variables, and proposes that further trials are required to properly inform young women of the risks.
Prophylactic oophorectomy in women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations also appears to reduce the risk of developing breast cancer.

Chemoprevention options include tamoxifen, raloxifene and exemestane (Aromasin). Lasofoxifene in a 0.5 mg dose reduced the likelihood of invasive breast cancer as well (1.6 vs. 0.2/1000 patient years, NNT = 143 over 5 years).

The largest trial of tamoxifen showed that for every 1000 women treated with tamoxifen for 5 years, we would prevent 18 breast cancers and 2 breast cancer deaths but cause 7 cases of invasive endometrial cancer, 2 strokes, 2 pulmonary emboli, and 2 deep venous thromboses. There was no impact on all-cause mortality.

The IBIS-II trial randomised nearly 4000 post-menopausal women at increased risk for breast cancer to anastrozole or placebo daily for 5 years. It demonstrated a 49% relative reduction in the risk of breast cancer in the active treatment arm. The absolute risk reduction was clinically important: 4.4% vs. 8.5% over the duration of the study, p <0.001, NNT = 25 to prevent one cancer over 5 years.

In the RUTH trial, for every 1000 women taking raloxifene there were 6 fewer invasive breast cancers and 6 to 7 fewer clinical vertebral fractures but 4 to 5 additional strokes and 6 episodes of venous thromboembolism. A systematic review of selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) concluded that the likelihood of developing breast cancer was reduced (NNT = 48) but that mortality was not affected.
Tamoxifen and raloxifene were similarly effective for reducing the risk of ER-positive and invasive breast cancer in postmenopausal women. All cause mortality and quality of life were similar.

In a randomized trial with 4560 high-risk postmenopausal women (Gail score ≥1.66%, age ≥60, prior hyperplasia, or DCIS), exemestane reduced the risk of invasive breast cancer after median 3-year follow-up (0.19% vs. 0.55%, P = .002, NNT = 93 for 3 years to prevent 1 breast cancer). There was no difference in deaths or quality of life; treatment discontinuation was more common with exemestane than placebo (NNH = 20), mostly due to hot flashes.

In discussing chemoprevention, women should be informed that the absolute risk reduction likely varies by risk factors for breast cancer and must be balanced against the potential harms; all cause mortality might not be reduced. They should also know that paroxetine appears to block the effect of tamoxifen on breast cancer prevention (NNH = 7).

A recent RCT of 3088 women between the ages of 18 and 70 years previously treated for early-stage breast cancer who consumed a diet high in vegetables and fiber and low in fat showed no significant differences in the recurrence of breast cancer or in breast cancer mortality compared with women who ate their usual diet.
A single prospective cohort study set in China found that greater consumption of soy protein was inversely associated with the risk of breast cancer recurrence.
Bisphosphonates and denosumab reduce the likelihood of fracture in women with breast cancer and bony metastases. There is no evidence that they prolong survival.
Meta-analysis of 18,776 patients with early breast cancer who received adjuvant bisphosphonate therapy does support reduction in subsequent recurrence in bone.
Adjuvant denosumab in early stage disease in postmenopausal women being treated with aromatase inhibitors has been shown to reduce the risk of clinical fracture.

A Cochrane review of 44 RCTs with a total of 37,302 women suggests that bisphosphonates given adjuvantly in early breast cancer can reduce the risk of subsequent bone metastases and increase overall survival, although this benefit seems clearer in the post-menopausal population.
A placebo-controlled trial in over 3000 women failed to show benefit for daily aspirin in reducing risk of breast cancer recurrence or improving survival.

Excisional biopsy or large core biopsy is recommended for all palpable solid lesions. Image-guided large core breast biopsy is the procedure of choice for nonpalpable lesions or abnormal breast calcifications. B
Ultrasound, CT scan, and MRI are used adjunctively in the diagnosis of breast abnormalities. B

list.listitem: The American College of Radiology Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System is as follows: Category 0 = incomplete; 1 = negative; 2 = benign; 3 = probably benign; 4 = suspicious abnormality; 5 = highly suspicious of malignancy; 6 = known biopsy-proven malignancy.

Breast symptoms associated with breast cancer include thickening, swelling, distortion, tenderness, skin irritation, overlying scaliness, and nipple abnormality with or without ulceration, retraction, or spontaneous discharge.

Breast masses more likely to be cancer have the following characteristics: fixed, firm, hard, and asymmetrical; attached to the deep skin or fascia (nonmobile); associated nipple dimpling or retraction; irregular, nondistinctive edges and borders; and noncystic or not soft. Other findings may include brown or bloody nipple discharge and axillary node tenderness and/or enlargement.
The overall clinical examination is fairly specific but not very sensitive. It is therefore better at ruling in cancer when the results are abnormal than ruling it out when the results are normal.
A validated clinical decision rule can predict the likelihood of breast cancer in women with breast symptoms.

Mammography is recommended as the initial test performed in evaluation of women with a breast lump, primarily for detection of additional abnormalities in the ipsilateral or contralateral breast. However, a normal mammogram result is not sufficient to rule out cancer and biopsy is needed for all solid masses.

Excisional or needle biopsy is recommended for all palpable solid breast lesions. Image-guided large core breast biopsy is the procedure of choice for nonpalpable lesions or abnormal breast calcifications. Ultrasound can be performed following an abnormal mammogram result to characterize an indeterminate lesion, especially in women younger than 30 years. Breast lesions meeting specific criteria (eg, palpable, cystic, and complex or septated in appearance) are appropriate for ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration.
Ductal hyperplasia with atypia or abnormal lesions that do not correlate with imaging or have questionable pathology should undergo repeat evaluation by excisional biopsy.
Women with spontaneous nipple discharge should undergo endocrine, mammogram, and ultrasound evaluations. Ductography use is controversial.

MRI is helpful in ruling out invasive disease in follow-up evaluation of a breast lump, postoperative scar, surgical margins, recurrence, high-risk patients with genetic mutations, or an abnormal mammogram result.

A nuclear medicine technique called molecular breast imaging that utilizes small semiconductor-based gamma-cameras in a mammographic configuration to provide breast images after injection of Tc-99m sestamibi, has a high sensitivity for the detection of small breast lesions. It has potential application as a screening adjunct in certain high-risk populations.
CT scan is more accurate but more expensive than ultrasound and scintigraphy in the detection of liver metastases.
Bone scan is highly sensitive in the evaluation of bone metastases.

The Gail Risk Model predicts the 5-year probability of breast cancer for women based on their personal risk factors. It has been prospectively validated and may be useful in chemoprophylaxis decision making.
A validated online calculator is available to determine if a woman is at sufficient risk for one of the BRCA mutations to require genetic counseling and possibly BRCA testing.
A clinical decision rule can predict the risk of breast cancer in women presenting to a primary care clinician with breast symptom.
Mammography is the initial test performed in evaluation of women with a breast lump for detection of additional tumors in the ipsilateral or contralateral breast.

Excisional biopsy or large core biopsy are recommended for all palpable lesions. Image-guided large core breast biopsy is recommended for nonpalpable lesions or abnormal breast calcifications to diagnose breast cancer. Adequate tissue for histology confirms diagnosis.
Ductal hyperplasia or abnormal lesions that do not correlate with imaging or have questionable pathology should undergo repeat evaluation by excisional biopsy.
Localized breast cancers are usually treated with lumpectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy (for staging purposes) and follow-up radiation therapy with or without chemotherapy or hormone therapy. B
Regional and metastatic breast cancers are treated with lumpectomy or mastectomy with lymph node dissection, followed by radiation, chemotherapy, and hormonal therapy. B

An RCT in 957 low risk ductal carcinoma in situ patients demonstrated that active surveillance is not inferior to surgery with or without radiation with a similar risk of subsequent invasive disease in both groups. B
The approach to the patient with breast cancer is shown in .
Surgical options for breast cancer should be discussed with patients (). There is no good evidence regarding timing of surgery during follicular or luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.

Lumpectomy (surgical removal of the tumor with clear margins) followed by radiation is recommended for localized breast cancers with similar survival rates to mastectomy. A pooled analysis of 6 trials confirmed comparable effects on mortality on long-term follow-up despite increased local and regional recurrence rates for breast-conserving therapy.

Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is preferred for most patients over complete axillary lymph node resection as a diagnostic tool to detect breast cancer spread beyond localized disease to minimize the risk of lymphedema (swelling under the arm).

A systematic review of 67 studies comparing axillary lymph node dissection with SLNB found less lymphedema (absolute difference 14%) and pain (absolute difference 24%) with SLNB. There was also less loss of strength with SLNB.

The INSEMA trial randomized 5502 women with T1 (90%) or T2 (tumor < 5 cm) to SNLB or no axillary surgery in a 4:1 ratio. After 6 years, no surgery was non-inferior to SNLB (5 year invasive disease free survival 91.9% for no surgery and 91.7% for SNLB). Axillary recurrence (1% vs 0.3%) and death (1.4% vs 2.4%) also were non-inferior.

A study randomized 2540 women to SNLB only or axillary lymph node dissection following detection of axillary macrometastases. Most had radiotherapy. SNLB alone was non-inferior to the more extensive surgery.

Mastectomy (complete removal of the breast) with removal of axillary lymph nodes (underarm lymph nodes) is recommended for nonlocalized disease and for staging purposes. Radiation, chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, and biologic therapy are adjunctive therapies to this approach.

There is no clear evidence regarding the benefits of immediate vs. delayed reconstruction following surgery for breast cancer. Delayed may be preferable following surgery for larger or high risk tumors where healing may delay adjuvant therapy.

A Cochrane review identified 11 studies with 2867 participants comparing prophylactic pre-operative or peri-operative antibiotics after breast cancer surgery with placebo. They found a reduction in the incidence of surgical site infection with pre-operative antibiotics (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.53-0.85).

A trial randomized 957 women with newly diagnosed low risk ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) defined as hormone receptor positive grade 1 or 2 without evidence of invasion. They were randomized to usual care (surgery with addition of radiation depending on type of surgery) or active surveillance which consisted of diagnostic mammography in the affected breast every 6 months and in the other breast every 12 months. At 2 years the rate of invasive cancer was 5.9% in the usual care group and 4.2% in the active surveillance (non-inferior).

A Cochrane review found that topical calendula (a homeopathic remedy) was more effective than a steroid containing cream in the treatment of radiotherapy induced dermatitis. A homeopathic mouthwash (Traumeel S) was more effective than placebo for stomatitis. The risk of bias was judged to be low in these studies.
Dance or movement therapy may have some benefit on quality of life in patients with cancer, although the evidence base is very limited.

There is suggestive but statistically inconclusive evidence from a trial of acupuncture versus sham acupuncture that patients may experience relief of aromatase inhibitor-induced arthralgia from the use of acupuncture.

In breast-cancer survivors with lymphedema, slowly progressive weight lifting may decrease exacerbations of lymphedema, reduce symptoms, and increase strength without significantly affecting limb swelling. This was confirmed in a randomized trial of 154 women treated for unilateral breast cancer, which found no increase in lymphedema among those randomized to upper body weight lifting and a possible benefit.
Exercise can improve range of motion in the shoulder for women who have undergone treatment with breast cancer.

The latest update of the NICE guidelines propose that exercise is discussed with patients at high risk of lymphoedema, as it appears to improve quality of life. There is still no clear evidence regarding whether it directly impacts lymphoedema risk.
Having a relationship with a primary care physician is associated with better outcomes for women with breast cancer.
In women with breast cancer who experience hot flushes, clonidine, SSRIs, SNRIs, gabapentin, and relaxation therapy are all effective.
In premenopausal women with hormone receptor-negative breast cancer, the addition of goserelin to standard chemotherapy reduced the likelihood of ovarian failure (8% vs. 22%; p = 0.04).

A systematic review of randomized trials found that beta-blockers, angiotensin receptor blockers, and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors attenuate the loss of left ventricular ejection fraction in patients being treated with trastuzumab or an anthracycline for breast cancer.

Following lumpectomy with sentinel nodel lymph biopsy, chemotherapy in combination with radiotherapy should be considered in the treatment of stage I and stage II breast cancer. Radiotherapy improves both local control and breast cancer-specific survival after localized breast conservation therapy. Preoperative chemotherapy may increase breast conservation rates, but leads to an increase in local recurrence rates. Adjuvant chemotherapy with taxanes improves survival in women with early breast cancer.

The INSEMA trial randomized 5502 women with T1 (90%) or T2 (tumor < 5 cm) to SNLB or no axillary surgery in a 4:1 ratio. After 6 years, no surgery was non-inferior to SNLB (5 year invasive disease free survival 91.9% for no surgery and 91.7% for SNLB). Axillary recurrence (1% vs 0.3%) and death (1.4% vs 2.4%) also were non-inferior.
The precise sequencing of adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy does not appear to affect outcomes, based on limited evidence from three RCTs.

There is some evidence that concurrent chemoradiation delivers improved disease-free and overall survival compared to sequential chemotherapy followed by radiation in patients with locally advanced disease after surgery.
A placebo controlled trial of daily aspirin in over 3000 patients with high risk nonmetastatic breast cancer determined that it did not reduce risk of recurrence or improve overall survival.
Use of a 21 gene essay in combination with tumor size and histologic grade can help target therapy in premenopausal women.

Radiotherapy may be omitted in carefully selected low risk women. A study in 500 women 55 and older with T1N0, tumor size < 2 cm, node negative grade 1 or 2 luminal A breast cancer omitted radiotherapy and followed them for 5 years, at which time recurrence was reported in only 2.3% and contralateral breast cancer was seen in 1.9%.

The SUPREMO trial identified women with stages pT1N1, pT2N1, pT3N0 or pT2N0 treated with mastectomy, axillary dissection and chemotherapy. They randomized 808 patients to chest wall irradiation or no radiation. After 10 years there was no difference in survival, disease-free survival, or metastatic-free survival.

Adjuvant polychemotherapy produces an absolute 10-year survival benefit of 7% to 11% for women younger than 50 years with early breast cancer, and 2% to 3% for women between the ages of 50 and 69 years unless their prognosis is already extremely good.

Hormone receptor positive, HER2-negative cancers in node negative patients do not obtain significant survival benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy according to a double blind RCT (TAILORx) although there may be specific subgroups on post-hoc analysis for whom chemotherapy is helpful. This is a useful addition to the literature combined with increasing use of Oncotype DX scores to predict the benefit of chemotherapy in individual cases.

With regard to specific cytotoxic agents in adjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer, a Cochrane review of 29 studies in 41,000 women concluded that the use of taxanes improves overall survival (hazard ratio 0.87) and also increases disease free survival.

The most recent update of the Early Breast Cancer Trialists Group undertook meta-analysis of 15 trials with over 18,000 patients finding a 14% reduction in risk of recurrence using the combination of anthracycline and taxane.

Increasing the dose intensity of adjuvant chemotherapy has also been demonstrated to reduce recurrence and improve survival in a meta-analysis of 26 RCTs looking at chemotherapy scheduling over a shorter time.

There is increasing evidence for the use of genomic risk prediction to guide decisions on adjuvant therapy. In selected patients endocrine therapy is non-inferior to chemoendocrine adjuvant therapy in improving disease-free survival. with ongoing clinical trials addressing selection of neo-adjuvant therapy on the basis of biomarker subtypes.

A study of a 21-gene breast cancer assay was useful for guiding selection of adjuvant chemotherapy in premenopausal women with 1-3 positive lymph nodes and a recurrence score of <= 25 based on the assay. Ia similar group of post-menopausal women, though, did not benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy.

A recent meta-analysis shows that aromatase inhibitors can be either an alternative or an adjuvant to tamoxifen for women with HR-positive tumors; options include anastrozole and exemestane following 2 to 3 years of tamoxifen (total = 5 years) or 5 years of letrozole following 5 years of tamoxifen. Patients taking aromatase inhibitors should be monitored for changes in bone mineral density and cardiovascular risk factors.

Ribociclib is a CDK4/6 inhibitor with proven efficacy in combination with aromatase inhibitors in the treatment of advanced breast cancer. A recent RCT in hormone sensitive, HER2 negative early stage disease has shown disease free survival benefit adding ribociclib to aromatase inhibitors.
In a trial comparing 5 years of letrozole following on from 2-3 years of tamoxifen against 2-3 years of letrozole there was significant improvement in progression free survival in the extended group.
Extending aromatase inhibitor therapy to ten years does increase progression free survival and reduce risk of contralateral breast cancer but without benefit on overall survival.

Recent data suggests reduced risk of recurrence of breast cancer at five years with use of exemestane and ovarian suppression in premenopausal women rather than tamoxifen with a trend towards increased benefit in the node negative population who had not received adjuvant chemotherapy.

Tamoxifen for 5 years after primary treatment improves the 10-year survival of women with ER-positive breast cancers and tumors of unknown status. A report of 20-year follow-up found the best survival in women treated with tamoxifen alone compared with radiation plus tamoxifen or radiation therapy alone (overall mortality 62%, 68%, and 71%, respectively), although women randomized to the combination therapy had a greater reduction of local and regional recurrence (5.3%) than those given tamoxifen alone (18.5%). Tamoxifen has been associated with ocular toxicity in 12%.

The ATLAS trial randomized women with early stage breast cancer who had received 5 years of tamoxifen to either 5 more years or no treatment. Women who were ER positive had a significant reduction in breast cancer recurrence (NNT = 36) and all cause mortality (NNT = 41). In a recent RCT of postmenopausal women with endocrine-responsive breast cancer, sequential treatment with letrozole and tamoxifen (2 years followed by 3 years) compared with 5 years of letrozole or tamoxifen monotherapy did not improve disease-free survival. There was no significant difference in overall survival between letrozole monotherapy and tamoxifen monotherapy.

The optimal duration of adjuvant aromatase inhibition was assessed in a trial of 3484 post-menopausal patients randomizing between 7 or 10 years of anastrozole therapy. Ten years increased risk of bone fracture without benefit on disease control rates.

In one study, the addition of zoledronic acid to adjuvant endocrine therapy in premenopausal patients with estrogen-responsive early breast cancer slightly increased 3-year disease-free survival (ARR 1%-3%).
Adjuvant irradiation of the regional nodes (internal mammary and medial supraclavicular) reduces the risk of local recurrence with uncertainty around overall survival benefit.

However an extensive review of all trials of regional node irradiation by the international Early Breast Cancer Trials Group categorised trials as pre or post 1980 and has shown that both breast cancer mortality and all cause mortality are reduced with regional node irradiation.

A trial omitting post-operative radiotherapy in women older than 65 years, with hormone sensitive, node negative tumours found no significant difference in 10 year survival but the local recurrence rate was significantly higher in the non-irradiated group.

A large trial of intra-operative radiation during lumpectomy versus post-operative external beam radiation has shown that there was no reduction in survival or increase in breast cancer mortality from the immediate intra-operative therapy.

Different methods of sequencing chemotherapy and radiotherapy do not seem to make a difference in breast cancer survival or recurrence if radiotherapy is initiated within 7 weeks of breast conservation therapy for early-stage localized breast cancer. A systematic review found that unconventional approaches to fraction size may improve outcomes. Using more than 2 Gy per fraction with shorter duration of therapy resulted in no difference in local recurrence, breast appearance, and 5-year survival. There was less acute skin toxicity with the unconventional approaches.

The non-inferiority of hypofractionated radiotherapy in early breast cancer has been confirmed by a Cochrane review including 9 RCTs with a total of 8228 patients. The shorter course radiotherapy seems best suited to tumours <3 cm in small to medium size breasts where excision margins are clear.

Recent trials of accelerated radiotherapy schedules to the partial breast after lumpectomy have not established euqivalence with the standard whole breast irradiation schedules. However, a recent trial with over 4000 patients showed that a one week 5 day course of radiotherapy was not inferior compared to a three week course of treatment on the outcomes of local relapse and local effects.

A study identified 1641 women with T1 to T3 breast cancer (≤2 cm to >5 cm), N1, and M0 and level I or II axillary lymph nodes but no distant metastasis. After neoadjuvant chemotherapy they were all tumor free. They were then randomized to regional nodal irradiation or no regional nodal irradiation. Outcomes were similar between groups.

Standard practice in DCIS disease has been surgery followed by whole breast irradiation. There is recent evidence for improved 10 year relapse free survival (97% vs 92%) with the addition of local boost to the tumor bed after conservative surgery.
Monoclonal antibody therapy holds great promise for the treatment of women with HER2/neu-positive breast cancers following adjuvant chemotherapy.

In women with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative tumors, adding bevacizumab to a regimen of epirubicin and cyclophosphamide followed by docetaxel improves outcomes (18.4% pathologic complete response vs. 14.9%; NNT = 33), especially among women who have triple negative tumors (estrogen, progesterone and HER2; 39% vs. 28%; NNT = 9). Adding the drug was not effective in HER2-positive cancers.

In women with early stage HER2-positive cancers, a trial randomized 3222 women to either doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide followed by docetaxel every 3 weeks, the same regimen with the addition of trastuzumab, or docetaxel and carboplatin plus 52 weeks of trastuzumab. Disease free 5 year survival rates were 75%, 84%, and 81% respectively; both of the regimens containing trastuzumab were better than the one not including the drug. In HER2-negative patients treated with neo-adjuvant chemotherapy who still have residual tumour at resection a recent large RCT of 910 patients demonstrated PFS and overall survival benefit from use of adjuvant capecitabine post-op.

Trastuzumab significantly improves overall survival in women with early stage HER2-positive tumors. The primary toxicity is congestive heart failure. An uncontrolled study in women with stage 1 node-negative HER2-positive breast cancer gave paclitaxel and trastuzumab for 12 weeks, followed by 9 months of trastuzumab alone and found 98.7% 3-year survival free of invasive disease.

The further addition of pertuzumab to trastuzumab in adjuvant therapy of early stage HER2-positive breast cancer increases disease free survival. A trial randomized 4805 women with early stage HER2-positive cancer to pertuzumab or placebo in addition to standard chemotherapy and 1 year of adjuvant trastuzumab. The treatment group had a small reduction in the likelihood of disease recurrence (7.1% vs. 8.7%; p = 0.045) and in 3-year invasive disease-free survival among those with node-positive disease (92.0% vs. 90.2%; p = 0.02), although there was no reduction in 3-year disease-free survival in those with node negative cancer.

In women with HER2-positive early stage breast cancer who had residual disease in the breast or axilla after neoadjuvant treatment with taxane-based chemotherapy and trastuzumab, those receiving 14 cycles of trastuzumab emtansine had improved overall survival (89% vs 84%).

An especially poor prognosis group are those patients with triple negative disease: negative for both hormone receptors and for HER2. The strategy of neo-adjuvant chemotherapy has been used to attempt better control for these aggressive tumours prior to surgery and the recent advent of immunotherapy options has given some hope. Adding pembrolizumab to standard neo-adjuvant chemotherapy in patients with early triple negative breast cancer increased the pathological complete response rate at surgery from 51.2% to 64.8% in one trial. Longer term follow-up of this trial found higher overall survival in the pembrolizumab group (87% vs 82%).

If triple negative patients have combined positive score for PDL1 sensitivity greater than 10, they are particularly likely to benefit from the addition of pembrolizumab to chemotherapy. A recent trial with 847 patients showed survival benefit in the CPS10 group from 16 month overall survival to 23 months with the addition of pembrolizumab.

Similarly the addition of atezolizumab to neo-adjuvant chemotherapy increased pathological CR rate in another trial from 41% to 58%. The follow-on from these studies been to look at addition of immunotherapy in the treatment of advanced and metastatic disease. The IMpassion trial adding atezolizumab or placebo to taxol in locally advanced triple negative disease failed to show improvement in progression free or overall survival.

Gemcitabine in combination with paclitaxel is indicated as an option for the treatment of metastatic breast cancer when docetaxel either as monotherapy or in combination with capecitabine is appropriate. Data regarding short vs. long infusion times for paclitaxel are limited, although shorter duration infusions (3 hours) appear to be associated with less toxicity.
High-dose chemotherapy with bone marrow or stem cell transplantation should not be given as clinical treatment for women with metastatic breast cancer.

Combination chemotherapy in the treatment of metastatic breast cancer shows a statistically significant improvement in response time and tumor response compared with single-agent chemotherapy. However, the addition of chemotherapy agents to a current regimen of 2 breast cancer chemotherapy agents for metastatic disease is associated with an increase in drug toxicities, a small improvement in overall tumour response (OR 1.2, 95% CI 1.01-1.4) but no clinical difference in survival time or in time to progression.

Platinum containing regimens do not improve survival, have significant toxicity, and are not recommended as treatment for metastatic cancer based on a systematic review of 12 RCTs. The exception is metastatic disease of triple negative subtype which is a poor prognostic group where there does appear to be benefit in progression free survival with platinum chemotherapy.

in a recent trial comparing chemotherapy in metastatic triple negative patients to a new antibody-drug conjugate sacituzumab govitecan, the median survival increased from 6.7 to 12.2 months with the new agent.

Sacituzumab govitecan was also evaluated in a RCT of 558 patients with untreated, advanced triple-negative breast cancer. Patients were randomized to sacituzumab govitecan or standard chemotherapy and progression-free survival was somewhat longer with sacituzumab govitecan (9.7 vs 6.9 months, p < .001).

Tamoxifen and toremifene were similarly effective for the treatment of advanced breast cancer, based on a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs with 2061 patients. Compared with endocrine therapies (eg, tamoxifen), third-generation aromatase inhibitors (eg, anastrozole, exemestane, letrozole) show statistically significant progression-free survival and clinical benefit in women with advanced metastatic breast cancer while showing an overall survival benefit. Decreased rates of thromboembolic events and vaginal bleeding are associated with aromatase inhibitors compared with endocrine therapies. Similar rates of hot flushes, arthralgias, osteopenia, nausea, and vomiting are observed among these agents. Endocrine therapy is similarly effective (although the body of evidence is limited) and less toxic than chemotherapy for women with metastatic breast cancer.

A study identified 521 women with hormone receptor positive/HER2 negative advanced breast cancer who had progressed or relapsed with previous endocrine therapy. They were randomized to palbociclib plus fulvestrant or fulvestrant alone. Median overall survival was higher in the combination therapy group (34.9 vs. 28.0 months, p <0.05). However, there was no statistically significant difference in overall survival.

A study identified 708 patients with hormone receptor–positive, HER2 negative advanced breast cancer who had relapsed or experienced disease progression after treatment with an aromatase inhibitor +/- CDK4/6 inhibitor. They were randomized to capivasertib + fulvestrant or placebo + fulvestrant. Progression free survival was longer in the intervention group (7.2 monts v 3.6 months, p < 0.0001).

Imlunestrant is a continuous estrogen receptor inhibitor. In a trial of 874 women with ER positive HER negative advanced breast cancer that had recurred, women were randomized to standard hormonal therpay, imlunestrant or imlunestrant + abemaciclib. Progression free survival was improved most with the combination therapy.

Camizestrant is a selective estrogen receptor degarder and complete ER antagonist. These researchers identified patients with advanced ER+ / HER2- tumors with ESR1 mutations and randomized them to camizestrant 75 mg + CDK4/6 inhibitor or CDK4/6 inhibitor plus another aromatase inhibitor. Those receiving camizestrant had longer progression free survival (16 vs 9.2 months, p < 0.001).

Vepdegestrant is another estrogen receptor degrader. A trial randomized 624 patients with advanced ER+ / HER2- tumors to vepdegestrant or fulvestrant. The median progression-free survival was greater with vepdegestrant (5.0 vs 2.1 months, p < 0.001).

A systematic review found that the vascular-endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitor bevacizumab in patients with refractory metastatic breast cancer improved response rates compared to placebo, but did not reduce mortality.

In a randomized trial with 302 patients who had a BRCA mutation and HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, those receiving olaparib had a longer period of progression-free survival than those receiving usual care (7 months vs. 4.2 months), a higher response rate (60% vs. 29%) and fewer adverse events (5% vs. 8% discontinuation).

An RCT identified 991 women with locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer who had been previously treated with trastuzumab and a taxane. They were randomized to either trastuzumab emtansine or lapatinib plus capecitabine. Progression free survival was significantly better in the trastuzumab group (9.6 months vs. 6.4 months) as was the hazard ratio for progression or death from any cause (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.55-0.77). Thrombocytopenia and elevated transaminases were more common with trastuzumab emtansine, but diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting were less common.

In an RCT of 808 women with metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer, half received trastuzumab + docetaxel + placebo, and half received trastuzumab + docetaxel + pertuzumab. The drugs were given until disease progressed or they developed intolerable side effects. Progression free survival was significantly better in the pertuzumab group (18.5 months vs. 12.4 months) as was the hazard ratio for progression or death (0.62; 95% CI 0.51-0.75). There was a trend toward lower all-cause mortality in the pertuzumab group. A subsequent follow-up of the same study showed improved overall survival in the pertuzumab group (56.5 months vs. 40.8 months; HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.56-0.84). Median progression free survival was also 6.3 months longer in the pertuzumab group.
A further study of adjuvant olaparib (PARP inhibitor) in BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutated patients confirmed significant benefit in 3 year disease free survival for addition of olaparib.

In a study of 431 women with BRCA mutation and advanced breast cancer, those randomized to talazoparib in addition to usual care had longer median progression free survival (8.6 months vs. 5.6months, p <0.001) than those randomized to placebo. Patient reported quality of life was also improved, with a trend toward reduced mortality.

In women with advanced HER2 negative breast cancer, addition of the cyclin dependent kinase (CDK4/6) inhibitor ribociclib to endocrine therapy resulted in increased overall survival (at 42 months 70.2% vs. 46.0%, p = 0.01, NNT = 3).

Another RCT compared letrozole plus either ribociclib or placebo in 668 women with HER-negative advanced breasat cancer. Overall survival after a median 6.6 years was 64 months in the ribociclib group vs 51 months with placebo (p < 0.008). Mortality at 6.6 years was also significantly lower (54% vs 66%, NNT = 8).

A cohort study identified 184 women with metastatic HER2 positive breast cancer who had previously been treated with trastuzumab emtansine. They were given trastuzumab deruxtecan and a response to therapy was reported in 61% for a median of 14.8 months.

A RCT identified 480 women with metastatic HER2 positive breast cancer who had disease progression after therapy with trastuzumab, pertuzumab, and trastuzumab emtansine. They were randomized to the oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor tucatinib or placebo, in combination with trastuzumab and capecitabine. Overall survival at 2 years was better in the tucatinib group (44.9% vs. 26.6%, p = 0.005, NNT = 5). The benefit was also seen in patients with brain metastases. Adverse events included diarrhea, rash, nausea, fatigue, and vomiting.

An RCT randomized 557 women with previously treated HER2-low cancer (expressing low levels of HER-2) to trastuzumab deruxtecan or the treating physician's choice of chemotherapy. Progression free survival and overall survival (23.4 months vs 16.8 months, p = 0.001) were both improved with trastuzumab.

A study identified 866 patients with hormone receptor–positive metastatic breast cancer with low HER2 expression and previous endocrine-based therapy but no previous chemotherapy. They were randomized to trastuzumab deruxtecan of physician's selection of chemotherapy. Progression free survival was longer in the trastuzumab group (13 vs 8 months).

An RCT randomized 325 women with PIK3CA-mutated advanced breast cancer to inavolisib (a PIK3CA inhibitor) or placebo. Progression free survival was more likely with inavolisib (15 vs 7.3 months), with drug discontinued due to adverse events in 6.8% vs 0.6% placebo.

Women with PIK3CA-mutated, ER–positive, HER2-negative locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer with recurrence or progression were randomized to receive inavolisib plus palbociclib–fulvestrant or placebo plus palbociclib–fulvestrant. The inavolisib group had better overall survival (34 vs 27 months).

Bisphosphonates (oral or IV) reduce bone pain; the risk, rate, and time to a skeletal event in women with advanced breast cancer; and clinically evident bone metastases. Timing of initiation and duration of bisphosphonate treatment for skeletal events is uncertain.
Early breast cancer detection and treatment improve prognosis and survival. B

Prognostic factors include the location and spread of tumor, presence or absence of hormone receptors, genetic factors, tumor size and shape, rate of cell division, and biologic markers; these factors are used to determine treatment options and possibility for cure. B
Poor prognosis is associated with 'triple negative' disease: patients in whom ER and PR homrone status is negative as well as HER2 negative.
Untreated disease progresses to regional and metastatic disease to liver, lung, and bone.

Complications and comorbidities include debility and significant limitations in basic activities of daily living, pain, psychosocial impairment, depression, infection, thromboembolism, edema, ascites, small bowel obstruction, pulmonary disease, and cardiac disease.
Five-year survival is 90% for localized disease, 83% for regional spread, and 26% for metastatic disease.
Overall, 88% of women with breast cancer will survive at least 10 years; 25% of recurrences and half of new cancers occur in the opposite breast after 5 years.

Prognostic factors include the location of tumor (outside or middle) and extent of disease spread, HR-positive (slow-growing) or HR-negative (more aggressive) status, HER2/neu status (more aggressive), high angiogenesis growth, genetic factors, tumor size and shape, rate of cell division, and biologic markers.
About two-thirds of the reduction in breast cancer mortality over time is due to advances in therapy and about one-third is attributable to mammographic screening.

A population based cohort study in Denmark of almost 6000 women demonstrated increased risk of mortality in premenopausal non-metastatic breast cancer in those with lower socioeconomic position, postulated to be due to possible underdetection of recurrence.

Perform 6- and 12-month follow-up clinical examination and mammographic studies for stable breast changes noted on mammogram in the first year and then annual mammogram screening for 3 years before resuming health maintenance screening per USPSTF guidelines. There is no evidence, however, that clinical examination confers a survival benefit over other methods of detection.
Yearly mammograms are advised for patients with Stage 0 to Stage III breast cancers with CBE every 4 to 6 months for 5 years.
Use of routine imaging and biomarkers is not recommended by NCCN guidelines, ASCO guidelines, or based on a Cochrane review.
Advise routine clinical breast exam and adherence to USPSTF mammographic screening intervals.

Recommend individual risk assessment with active interventions to address modifiable risk factors (eg, physical inactivity, overweight, alcohol consumption) to promote healthier choices and risk awareness in women.
Reassure women that exposure to x-rays during mammography is minimal: 0.6 mSv, which is much less than the annual dose from background radiation (3.6 mSv).

In one RCT, patients receiving a psychologic intervention in addition to follow-up assessment only were found to have a reduced risk of breast cancer recurrence (24% vs. 29%) and death from breast cancer (HR = 0.44; P = .016) and death from all causes (HR = 0.51; P = .028) compared with patients in the assessment only arm.
Older women who undergo regular mammography are diagnosed at an earlier stage of disease and are less likely to die from their disease.

Although data are limited, the hazard rates for progression-free survival for older women with early breast cancer were 0.55 (95% CI 0.39-0.77) for surgery alone vs. primary endocrine therapy and 0.65 (95% CI 0.53-0.81) for surgery plus endocrine therapy vs. endocrine therapy alone; however, there were no differences in overall survival by treatment group.

Primary endocrine therapy should be offered to women who are unfit for or refuse surgery for ER-positive tumors. The clinical effectiveness of aromatase inhibitors in the primary treatment of ER-positive breast tumors in women 70 years or older is unknown.

Breast cancer occurs in 1 of every 3000 pregnant women, most often between the ages of 32 and 38 years. Diagnosis and staging should be performed by clinical examination, ultrasound, and mammogram with adjustments to limit exposure risk to the fetus.

There is no evidence that termination of pregnancy after a diagnosis of breast cancer is necessary, and treatment of breast cancer should not be delayed. Breast-conserving surgery and modified radical mastectomy are options for early-stage disease in pregnant women; reconstruction is often deferred.

Chemotherapy should not be given during the first 3 months of pregnancy as it increases risk of miscarriage. Chemotherapy is considered relatively safe for subsequent use but can cause low birth weight and preterm labor. The effectiveness of hormone therapy with or without chemotherapy in pregnant breast cancer patients is unknown. Radiation therapy can be used with appropriate shielding; if cancer is detected in the second trimester and is early stage, lumpectomy can be followed by chemotherapy and radiation treatment deferred until after birth.
Lactation should be stopped if chemotherapy is considered for treatment immediately postpartum because of the likelihood of passing on the anticancer drugs through breast milk.

Long-term survival after breast cancer does not appear to be affected by pregnancy. The effects of radiation and chemotherapy treatment on later pregnancies are unknown. Most doctors recommend a woman defer a pregnancy for 2 years following breast cancer treatment.

A study enrolled 516 women (mostly with stage I or II hormone receptor positive breast cancer) who desired pregnancy. Adjuvant hormone therapy was withheld and after 3 years there were 368 pregnancies and 317 women with at least one live birth. There were 44 breast cancer recurrences in over 1600 patient years of follow-up, which was no different from a comparison group that continued endocrine therapy.

feature_body.strong: For women who are not Ashkenazi Jews, these situations are of concern:

list.listitem: Breast cancer in family: - Bilateral (both breasts) breast cancer in a first-degree relative (mother, sister, daughter) - Breast cancer in 2 first-degree relatives—1 of whom was diagnosed by age 50 years or younger - Breast cancer in 3 or more first-degree or second-degree (aunt, cousin) relatives - Breast cancer in a male relative
Ovarian cancer in family: - Ovarian cancer in 2 or more first-degree or second-degree relatives
Breast and ovarian cancer in family: - Breast and ovarian cancer among first-degree and second-degree relatives - Both breast and ovarian cancer in a first-degree or second-degree relative
Breast or ovarian cancer in family: - Any first-degree relative or 2 second-degree relatives on the same side of the family
Breast or ovarian cancer and known BRCA mutation in family: - Breast or ovarian cancer diagnosed in the family and a relative is known to have a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation

feature_body.strong: For all women of Ashkenazi Jewish descent consider counselling if:

list.listitem: Any first-degree relative with breast or ovarian cancer
Two second-degree relatives on same side with breast or ovarian cancer
